newsitem.title: NEPAL: World Bank chief in Nepal for talks on economy.
newsitem.headline: World Bank chief in Nepal for talks on economy.

text.p: World Bank President James Wolfensohn arrived in Kathmandu on Wednesday on the first visit by the bank's chief to the Himalayan kingdom in nine years, officials said.
"The visit will focus on macro and sectoral policies for private sector development," the World Bank said in a statement.
Nepal liberalised its economy in 1992 to draw foreign capital into the kingdom's moribund economy and privatised 11 public enterprises in four years.
Bank officials said Wolfensohn's discussions with Nepali officials would focus on improving the quality of social services to the poor in Nepal, one of the world's 10 poorest countries.
"We will explain our economic policy to him," a spokesman for Nepal's finance ministry told Reuters.
Wolfensohn begins his visit with a meeting on Thursday with Prime Minister Sher Bahadur Deuba. He will also meet representatives of the donor community.
In the past donors have shown concern over poor project implementation and lack of counterpart funds which has hit development plans.
More than 60 percent of the kingdom's development budget comes from foreign aid including soft term loans from multilateral lending institutions including the World Bank.

Last year, the bank cancelled its aid support of $175 million for a $764 million hydro-electric project in the Arun valley in east Nepal. It said Nepal's institutional capability was not adequate for the project to succeed.

Water Resources Secretary Dwarika Nath Dhungel said Nepal would request the World Bank for funds to implement the upper Karnali hydro-electric project in west Nepal, which will have a capacity of 240 mega watts (MW).
Snow-fed rivers cascading from the Himalayas with combined potential to generate 83,000 MW of hydro-electricity make Nepal one of the world's richest countries in terms of water resources.
But the potential remains untapped as the country generates only 293 MW of electricity, which is available to just 15 percent of its 21 million people.
Wolfensohn will visit India for eight days from October 12.
